text: Hey, do you want to know why the majority of plane crash survivors are men? It's actually because they are the most willing to claw and trample whomever just to get to those exits. Yes, they've actually done a study on this. So the lady in the video basically makes two claims. First, that the majority of plane crash survivors are men. And second, which is in my opinion the main claim, is that this happens because men are the most willing to claw and trample whomever just to get to those exits. And for this, she uses a study from 1970 called Survival in Emergency Escape from Passenger Aircraft. She doesn't name the research in the video but it is mentioned in the comments. But before we even get into the study, it is worth noting that this report is more than 55 years old and it is not a study of all plane crashes in general. It is based on three specific aircraft evacuation accidents from the 1960s with 261 passengers in total. Out of those 261 passengers, 105 died while trying to escape during the short window before lethal smoke, heat, and toxic conditions build up inside the cabin. So even if everything she said was perfectly supported by the study, you still could use this to make a broad claim about all plane crashes, all passengers, or men in general. But the funny part is, even this study does not really support the main claim she is making. So what is the study actually about? It looks at three survivable aircraft accidents where impact itself was not the main killer. The planes were not completely destroyed on impact and the main danger came after the crash. Fire, smoke, toxic fumes, panic, and the need to evacuate very quickly. And yes, according to this study, adult men did survive at a higher rate. The fatality rate was about 34% for adult men, about 47% for adult women, and about 66% for children. So if someone says, in this study, men survived more often, that part is true. But the second claim, that this happened because men were the most willing to claw and trample whomever, is where the argument falls apart. Because that is not what the study says. The authors say that one of the most obvious factors was distance from the passenger seat to the exit they tried to use. In simple terms, if you were closer to a usable exit, you had a better chance. If you were farther away, or if you moved towards the wrong exit, your chances got worse. In the Denver accident, for example, all fatalities were in the second class, while first-class passengers all survived, and men were overrepresented in the first class. So in that case, part of the male advantage can be explained by where people were sitting, not by some dramatic fantasy where men were trampling women and kids like villains in a disaster movie. The authors also discuss other possible factors. One of them is physical strength. On average, men are larger and stronger than women. Women are larger and stronger than children. And younger adults tend to have better speed, strength, and agility than older adults. In an evacuation where people have seconds or minutes to reach an exit, that can obviously matter. But again, this is a physical and human factors explanation. It's not the same as saying men survived because they were morally worse people. The study also mentions other possible factors. Flying experience, because in the 1960s, men were more likely to be frequent air travelers. Panic behavior, such as whether people use the closest exit or follow the crowd. And even clothing, because women's clothing at time could be more restrictive and more flammable. So what do we have in the end? We have an old, limited study based on three specific evacuation accidents. We have evidence that adult men, especially younger adult men, survived at a higher rate in those cases. We also have evidence that seat location, distance to the exit, speed, strength, agility, experience, clothing, and behavior under stress may have played a role. What we do not have is proof that men survived because they were eager to claw and trample whomever just to get to those exits.
